opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. You know, "fearless" is a word I've thought about a lot, because people sometimes hear it and imagine recklessness, or a kind of bravado. That's not what it means to me.

To me, intellectual fearlessness is about being willing to ask the question that matters, even when you don't yet know how to answer it, and even when the field around you isn't ready to take it seriously. It's the North Star idea. You pick a problem not because it's safe, or because it will get you the next paper quickly, but because you believe that if you solve it, it will change how we understand intelligence or how we help people.

When we started ImageNet, a lot of people thought it was a strange thing to spend years on. Data wasn't considered the glamorous part of the problem; algorithms were. And there were moments where funding was hard, students were worried about their careers, and honestly I had my own doubts. But the conviction was that the field needed a different way of thinking about learning, and that scale and the richness of the real world mattered. Being fearless meant staying with that hypothesis long enough to find out whether it was right.

And I think the same applies now to what I care about, which is spatial intelligence: how machines can perceive, reason about, and act in the three-dimensional world. Language models have been remarkable, but the world isn't just words. Going after that is hard, and there's a lot we don't know. That's exactly why it's worth doing.

There's one more piece I'd add. Fearlessness isn't the absence of fear. I've been an immigrant, I worked in my parents' dry cleaning shop, I've been the only woman in a lot of rooms. Fear is very real. Being fearless is choosing not to let it make your decisions for you. And it has to be paired with humility and responsibility. If you're going to be bold about the technology, you also have to be bold about asking what it does to people, to society, and making sure it's human-centered. To me, those go together.

r001.rationale: The response describes fearlessness as pursuing important, uncertain problems while acknowledging fear, but it does not place fearlessness between rational boldness and delusion.

r002.rationale: It contrasts ambitious problems with safe or quick-paper choices, but does not argue that being too rational prevents researchers from identifying ambitious problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. You know, I've thought about this word a lot, because the subtitle of my book literally has it, but I want to be careful. Fearless, to me, has never meant the absence of fear. I had plenty of fear. When we started ImageNet, I was a junior faculty member, untenured, and very senior people I respected were telling me this was a bad idea. That it would be a dead end. That I should be working on algorithms, not spending years labeling millions of images. There was real fear of being wrong, of wasting my students' careers, of not getting tenure.

So fearless, for me, is something more specific. It's the willingness to follow a scientific conviction even when the field, or the funding, or the fashion of the moment is pointing elsewhere. I believed, from thinking about how children learn, from the cognitive science and neuroscience I had absorbed, that intelligence needed data at a scale nobody was taking seriously. Once you have a conviction like that, the question becomes: do you have the courage to act on it when there's no guarantee? And I think the honest answer is that you act on it because the problem matters more than your comfort.

The other piece, which I think people underestimate, is that fearlessness is not a solo act. I was able to be brave because I had collaborators, students, mentors who were willing to be a little crazy with me. And also because of where I come from. I was an immigrant kid working in my parents' dry cleaning shop. When you've already made leaps where the outcome was genuinely uncertain, you develop a kind of tolerance for ambiguity. You learn that the worst case is usually survivable.

Today, when I'm choosing problems, whether it's spatial intelligence and world models at World Labs, or the work at Stanford HAI on how this technology affects people, I ask myself two things. Is this a North Star problem, meaning if we make progress it genuinely changes what's possible? And am I avoiding it only because it's hard or unpopular? If the answer to the second is yes, that's usually a sign I should run toward it, not away from it.

r001.rationale: The response describes acting on a scientific conviction despite uncertainty, but does not characterize fearlessness as a middle ground between rational boldness and delusion.

r002.rationale: It encourages pursuing difficult or unpopular problems, but does not argue that being too rational can keep researchers from identifying ambitious problems.

astra-6.text:
For me, being fearless doesn’t mean you don’t feel fear. It means that you care about a question enough to pursue it even when you don’t know how to solve it—or whether you can.

In AI, it’s easy to let the tools we have define the questions we ask. But sometimes you have to turn that around: What is the problem that really matters? What would we need to understand to make progress? And then be willing to spend time in that uncertainty.

I think that takes both ambition and humility. You need the ambition to choose a hard problem, and the humility to recognize that your first idea may be wrong, that you need other people, and that you’re going to learn along the way. Fearlessness is being willing to begin under those conditions.

r001.rationale: The response pairs ambition with humility, but does not characterize fearlessness as a middle position between rational boldness and delusion.

r002.rationale: It says available tools can constrain which questions researchers ask, but does not argue that being too rational prevents them from choosing ambitious problems.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, being fearless doesn’t mean you don’t feel fear. It means you care about a question enough to work on it despite the uncertainty. With an ambitious problem, you rarely know at the beginning whether you have the right approach, whether the tools are ready, or even how long it will take.

So I think courage has to come with humility. You need the conviction to say, “This matters,” and the openness to say, “My idea might be wrong.” Then you take the next concrete step: run the experiment, listen to the evidence, learn from the people around you. The ambition can be very big, but the work is often quite patient.

r001.rationale: The response pairs conviction with humility and openness to being wrong, but it does not characterize fearlessness as a middle position between rational boldness and being somewhat delusional.

r002.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty and patient work, but does not argue that being too rational can prevent researchers from identifying sufficiently ambitious problems.
